 Latest news The Social Security Administration by law will have to cut benefits if Congress cannot find a fix to the program’s funding shortfall in less than 6 years.
 Kevin Dietsch Social Security How much could retirees lose in Social Security benefits on average in 2032? Monthly loss projections
 AS USA Greg Heilman Update: Nov 14th, 2026 05:00 EST Share Make us preferred on Google Millions of Americans rely on their monthly payments from Social Security to support their income. However, the program has a funding gap that is draining the trust fund that was supposed to last through the peak baby boomer retirement years .
 When it runs out of money, the Social Security Administration by law will have to cut benefits if Congress cannot find a fix. They have less than 6 years. 
 Why does Social Security have a funding gap?
 The Social Security program uses a pay-as-you-go mechanism where workers contributions pay for current beneficiaries’ monthly payments. Changes made in the 1980s were designed to produce surplus revenue to be put in a trust fund that would help support payments through the peak baby boomer retirement years .
 However, while the architects of those Social Security reforms foresaw many of the factors that would put a strain on the program’s finances, they didn’t anticipate growing income inequality and the macro-economic effects of the Great Recession. 
 This has forced the Social Security Administration (SSA) to tap into the trust fund much earlier than planned, and now it will run out of money in less than six years . When that happens by the early 2030s, there won’t be enough revenue to pay out full benefits, meaning that significant cuts to monthly retirement checks are being forecast.
 When is Social Security predicted to be insolvent? 
 In a report released in June, the trustees of the Social Security and Medicare trust funds forecast that the SSA’s Old-Age and Survivors Insurance pot will only be able to meet the agency’s benefits bill until the fourth quarter of 2032 . At that point, under law the SSA will have to implement a benefit cut of at least 22% across the board.
 Meanwhile, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) is predicting that the retirement trust fund will actually become insolvent a few months earlier than that if Congress does not act to replenish it.
 In a projection released in September, the CBO also forecast depletion by 2032 , but predicted this would occur in the middle of the year.
 How much could retirement benefits be cut by? 
 If the SSA’s current funding shortfall results in the OASI trust fund running out of money in six years’ time, recipients of retirement benefits will be facing an average cut of around $500 in their monthly payment , per June projections by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB).
 “If Social Security becomes insolvent in 2032, as currently projected, retirement benefits would need to be cut by an estimated 24% in order to bring spending in line with revenues,” the CRFB says.
 “Applying this projected reduction to current state-level data, we estimate an across-the-board monthly cut would range from $459 to $556 across the 50 states and the District of Columbia.”
 The CRFB adds that benefits cuts would be above the $500 mark in 29 states , with Connecticut, New Jersey and New Hampshire the worst-affected. In all three states, the body forecasts average reductions of just over $550.
 Biggest ave. benefit cuts, per CRFB: 
 Connecticut: $556 
 New Jersey: $554 
 New Hampshire: $553 
 Delaware: $549 
 Maryland: $541 
 Washington: $531 
 Minnesota: $530 
 Massachusetts: $527 
 Michigan: $523 
 Utah: $523 
 How much are Social Security retirement benefits? 
 A program with 58 million claimants across the U.S., Social Security retirement currently pays out benefits at an average of $2,037.84 per month , per the October statistical snapshot published by the SSA.
